_about: Pre/post concept test for Module 2 (virtual screening). 'answer' is the index of the correct option. Check the science before using with students.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of virtual screening?
options: To rank or filter a large compound library on the computer so that only a small number of promising compounds go to the lab
To prove that a compound is a safe medicine
To synthesise every compound in the library
To measure the real activity of every compound
questions.why: Virtual screening narrows millions of possibilities to a short list that is affordable to buy and test. It predicts, it does not prove.

questions.q: Why is virtual screening usually done as a funnel of stages?
options: Cheap, fast filters remove many compounds first, so the slow and more accurate methods only run on the survivors
Because computers can only run one method at a time
Because every stage must remove exactly half the compounds
Because docking cannot be run on more than 100 compounds
questions.why: Each stage trades speed for accuracy. Putting the quick filters first saves time and money.

questions.q: Lipinski's rule of five (molecular weight, cLogP, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors) is used to…
options: flag compounds that are unlikely to be good oral drugs, as a guide rather than a law
prove that a compound binds the target
predict the exact dose of a drug
find the 3D shape of a protein
questions.why: The rules describe the property range of most oral drugs. Many successful drugs break one of them, so they are a guide.

questions.q: A strict property filter removes some compounds that are actually active. These lost compounds are called…
options: false negatives
false positives
decoys
duplicates
questions.why: A false negative is a real hit that the method wrongly rejects. Filters that are too strict create them.

questions.q: Why do we prepare a library before screening (remove salts and duplicates, set charges, generate 3D shapes, flag PAINS)?
options: Methods need correct, clean 3D molecules, and messy structures give misleading scores
To make the library bigger
To remove all compounds that bind the target
Preparation is optional and changes nothing
questions.why: Docking and shape methods work on the 3D structure in the right charge state. Bad input gives bad rankings. PAINS are scaffolds that often look active in many assays for the wrong reasons.

questions.q: Which statement about ligand-based and structure-based screening is correct?
options: Ligand-based needs at least one known active to compare with; structure-based needs a 3D structure of the target
Both need the same inputs
Ligand-based needs a protein structure; structure-based needs a known drug
Neither needs any prior knowledge
questions.why: Ligand-based methods ask 'which compounds look like a known active?'. Structure-based methods ask 'which compounds fit the pocket?'.

questions.q: A weakness of ranking only by similarity or shape to one known drug is that it…
options: tends to miss active compounds that have a different scaffold
always finds every active compound
cannot rank large libraries
only works for proteins
questions.why: Compounds that bind the same pocket in a different way look different from the reference, so a similarity search can miss them. Using more than one method helps.

questions.q: The enrichment factor at 10% (EF10) is 3. What does this mean?
options: The top 10% of the ranked list contains 3 times more actives than a random 10% would
3 compounds were active
The method is 3% accurate
The top 3 compounds are active
questions.why: EF compares the hit rate in the selected top fraction with the hit rate of the whole library. Values above 1 mean better than random.

questions.q: A ROC curve has an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.5. What does this say about the ranking?
options: It is no better than random
It is perfect
It is slightly worse than perfect
It has found half of the actives
questions.why: AUC 0.5 is random ranking and 1.0 is perfect. Real screens usually sit in between, so we also check early enrichment.

questions.q: After the screen, you have a ranked list of the top 100 compounds. What should you do before testing them?
options: Inspect them: poses and interactions, PAINS and property alerts, and chemical diversity, then pick a manageable and varied set
Send all 100 to the lab at once
Pick only the 10 most similar to each other
Trust the scores and skip any inspection
questions.why: Screening scores are predictions. A short, diverse, inspected list gives the lab the best chance of finding real hits.
